lead: A 1024×1024 grey image at 8 bits per pixel is 1 MiB of raw data, and a phone photo is many such images. Most of those bits repeat information. Image compression measures that repetition as coding, interpixel and psychovisual redundancy, then removes as much as the user allows. The result is smaller files for storage, faster uploads on slow links, and fewer bytes sent over a network. This chapter sets up the vocabulary, the ratios and the entropy limit that the actual coders obey.
prereq: You need: bits per pixel from Unit 1, Sampling and quantization, and the encoder is the reverse of the degradation path in 3.1.

sections.h3: Why an image file is large

blocks.text: Raw image size is rows × columns × bits per pixel. A 1024×1024 grey image at 8 bits per pixel needs 1024×1024×8 = 8,388,608 bits, which is 1 MiB. A colour image triples that. Sending millions of such images is expensive, so we compress.
Compression works because most of those bits repeat information. Three kinds of repetition are recognised.

items: Coding redundancy: the code words are longer than the symbol probabilities require. A fixed 8-bit code for a pixel value that appears 90% of the time wastes bits.
Interpixel redundancy: neighbouring pixels are correlated. A sky patch has almost the same value at (x,y) and (x+1,y).
Psychovisual redundancy: the eye does not see all fine detail equally. Removing detail the eye cannot notice saves bits but changes the image.

blocks.text: Lossless compression removes only the first two. Lossy compression also removes the third, so it can reach much smaller files.

blocks.where: b is the original number of bits, B is the compressed number of bits, and C is the compression ratio. C = 4 means the file is one quarter of the original size.
R is the relative data redundancy, a fraction between 0 and 1. C = 4 gives R = 0.75, so 75% of the original data was redundant.

blocks.text: Bits per pixel = total bits / (M × N), where M is the number of rows and N is the number of columns. A 1 MiB image at 1024×1024 has 8 bits per pixel. After compression to 256 KiB it has 2 bits per pixel.
Lossless means the decoder reproduces every pixel exactly. Lossy means pixels change, so we need a fidelity measure.

blocks.where: f(x,y) is the original pixel, g(x,y) is the decoded pixel, M rows and N columns. Lower MSE means better quality.
MAX is the largest possible pixel value, for example 255 for 8-bit images. PSNR is in decibels (dB), and higher is better.

blocks.text: SNR compares signal power to error power: SNR = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(σ<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup> / σ<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup>), where σ<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup> is the variance of the original image and σ<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> is the variance of the error. Higher SNR means better quality.

sections.h3: The source encoder and the entropy limit

blocks.text: A source encoder has three blocks: mapper, quantizer and symbol coder. The decoder runs them in reverse.

items: Mapper: transforms pixels to reduce interpixel redundancy. It is reversible. Prediction and the DCT are mappers.
Quantizer: rounds values to reduce psychovisual redundancy. It is the only lossy step.
Symbol coder: gives short code words to likely symbols to reduce coding redundancy. It is lossless. Huffman coding is in 3.8.

blocks.where: p<sub>i</sub> is the probability of symbol i, and H is the entropy in bits per symbol. No lossless code can average fewer than H bits per symbol.

blocks.text: If four symbols have probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125, then H = 1.75 bits per symbol. A fixed 2-bit code uses 2 bits for every symbol; an entropy coder can approach 1.75.
Predictive coding and transform coding are the practical mappers; they are in 3.9. This chapter only fixes the model and the limits.

figure.caption: The worked example runs down the source encoder: a 1 MiB image at 8 bits per pixel leaves as a 256 KiB bitstream at 2 bits per pixel, so C = 4 and R = 0.75. Only the quantizer is lossy; the symbol coder aims for the 1.75 bits per symbol entropy limit, below the fixed 2-bit code.

spec.title: Source encoder
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom source encoder chain: a 1024×1024 8-bit image of 1 MiB passes through a mapper for interpixel redundancy, a lossy quantizer for psychovisual redundancy, and a symbol coder for coding redundancy, producing a 256 KiB output at 2 bits per pixel with C = 4, R = 0.75 and entropy limit 1.75 bits per symbol.

examples.question: A 1024×1024 8-bit grey image is compressed to a 256 KiB file. (a) Find the original bits, the compressed bits, the compressed bits per pixel, the compression ratio C and the relative data redundancy R. (b) Four symbols have probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125. Find the entropy H.
steps: Compressed bits per pixel = 2,097,152 / (1024 × 1024) = 2 bits per pixel.
Relative data redundancy R = 1 − 1/C = 1 − 1/4 = 0.75, which is 75%.
0.125 × log<sub>2</sub>(1/0.125) = 0.125 × 3 = 0.375 bits, and this appears twice, so 0.75 bits.
examples.answer: C = 4, R = 0.75 (75% redundant), the compressed image is 2 bits per pixel, and H = 1.75 bits per symbol.
examples.check:
import math
w = 1024
h = 1024
orig_bits = w * h * 8
print(orig_bits)
print(orig_bits // 8)
comp_bytes = 256 * 1024
comp_bits = comp_bytes * 8
print(comp_bits)
bpp = comp_bits / (w * h)
print(bpp)
C = 8 / bpp
print(C)
R = 1 - 1 / C
print(R)
p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125]
H = -sum(pi * math.log2(pi) for pi in p)
print(H)

traps: C and R are different numbers for the same file. C = 4 means R = 0.75, not R = 4 and not R = 75.
Entropy uses log<sub>2</sub> because the answer is in bits per symbol. Using log<sub>10</sub> gives a smaller number in the wrong unit.
Keep b and B in the same unit inside C = b / B. Do not divide original bits by compressed bytes.
Lossless compression cannot average below the entropy H. A claim of lossless compression below H is impossible, not just difficult.
PSNR is in dB and higher is better; MSE is lower when the image is better. Do not say a low PSNR means good quality.

quiz.q: Define coding redundancy and state its cause.
quiz.a: Coding redundancy is the extra bits used because code words are longer than the symbol probabilities require. It happens when a fixed-length code is used for symbols that occur with very different probabilities.

quiz.q: Why can a lossless coder not average fewer than H bits per symbol?
quiz.a: H is the average information per symbol. A lossless decoder must distinguish every symbol exactly. Any code that averaged fewer than H bits would leave some symbols indistinguishable or would violate the information bound, so H is the lower limit.

quiz.q: A 512×512 8-bit grey image is compressed to 128 KiB. Find the compressed bits per pixel, C and R.
A method claims lossless compression with C = 10 on an 8-bit image whose measured entropy is 3 bits per pixel. Is the claim possible? Explain.
quiz.a: C = 10 means the compressed rate is 8/10 = 0.8 bits per pixel. A lossless coder cannot go below the entropy of 3 bits per pixel. So the claim is impossible; either the method is lossy or the entropy was measured wrongly.

quiz.q: Four symbols have probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. Find the entropy H in bits per symbol.
Which block in the source encoder is the only lossy step, and which redundancy does it target?
quiz.a: The quantizer is the only lossy step. It targets psychovisual redundancy by rounding away detail that the eye does not notice.

quiz.q: Write the PSNR formula and define MAX.
quiz.a: PSNR = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(MAX<sup>2</sup> / MSE). MAX is the largest possible pixel value, such as 255 for an 8-bit image.

quiz.q: Why does psychovisual redundancy allow lossy compression but not lossless compression?
quiz.a: Psychovisual redundancy is detail the human eye does not notice. Removing it changes pixel values, so the decoder cannot reproduce the original exactly. Lossless compression must keep every pixel value, so it can remove only coding and interpixel redundancy.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the same three redundancies drive JPEG and PNG for still images, H.264 and HEVC for video, and DICOM storage for medical scans. Newer formats such as WebP and AVIF trade more computation for smaller files. Search for rate-distortion optimisation, entropy coding, and JPEG XL if you want the modern design view.
